parsed_answer.content: Scaling WebSockets in a distributed environment presents a unique challenge: the stateful nature of the TCP connection. Unlike stateless HTTP, where any load balancer can route a request to any server, a WebSocket connection is pinned to a specific server instance. When you have multiple instances of your application, a client connected to Server A cannot receive a message pushed by a process running on Server B because the connection context only exists on Server A. This is where a Pub/Sub backplane becomes mandatory. By introducing a message broker like Redis or Kafka, you decouple the message producer from the connection handler. When an event occurs, the application publishes a message to the backplane, and every instance of your WebSocket service subscribes to that channel, broadcasting the payload to the locally connected clients.

items: Connection Affinity: Use sticky sessions at the Load Balancer level to ensure the initial HTTP handshake and subsequent WebSocket upgrade stay on the same node, though the backplane handles the cross-node communication logic.

Redis Pub/Sub Mechanics: Redis maintains a list of subscribers per channel. When a message is published, Redis iterates through the subscriber list and pushes the message to each client's socket buffer. This is highly efficient for ephemeral data.

Kafka Consumer Groups: In a WebSocket cluster, each server instance should ideally belong to a unique consumer group if you want every instance to receive every message, or share a group if you want to distribute load (though for broadcasting, you typically want every node to receive the message).

Backpressure and Buffer Management: When scaling, ensure your WebSocket handlers are non-blocking. If the backplane sends messages faster than the client can consume, the server's outbound buffer will grow, potentially leading to OutOfMemoryErrors.

parsed_answer.content: A common production pitfall is the 'Broadcast Storm.' If you have 100 nodes and 10,000 clients, publishing a single event to a global channel triggers 100 nodes to attempt to write to their respective local sockets simultaneously. Always implement a circuit breaker or a rate-limiter on your outbound message pipeline to prevent the WebSocket thread pool from saturating during peak traffic, which would otherwise cause a cascading failure across your cluster.

title: How to scale WebSockets? (Pub/Sub backplane with Redis/Kafka)
